dnsr: Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Model in R

Overview

The dnsr package provides a comprehensive implementation of the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model for yield curve modeling and analysis. It offers a complete workflow from data acquisition to model fitting, factor dynamics estimation, advanced stochastic simulation, and visualization.

Features

  • Data Acquisition: Download and process U.S. Treasury yield curve data, with retries and an optional on-disk cache
  • Model Calibration: Robust fitting of the DNS model to yield curve time series, numerically or by concentrated least squares
  • Factor Dynamics: Estimate the stochastic processes governing yield curve evolution, as independent factors or as a full VAR(1), with standard errors
  • Advanced Simulation: Generate future yield curve scenarios, either through YUIMA or by sampling the exact transition law
  • Pricing: Discount factors, zero-coupon prices and par yields off a fitted curve
  • Visualization: Create informative plots of yield curves and model results
  • Parallel Processing: Support for faster model fitting with multiple cores
  • Bundled data: A six-year Treasury panel, so everything above can be tried without an API key

Installation

dnsr is not on CRAN; install it from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ambientpointcorp/dnsr")

# For the SDE simulation paths, also install YUIMA (a Suggests dependency)
install.packages("yuima")

Setup

Before using the package, you need a free FRED API key to download Treasury data:

  1. Get a FRED API key: Visit https://fred.stlouisfed.org/ and create a free account
  2. Request an API key: Go to https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/api_key.html
  3. Set your key:
# Option 1: Set for current session
Sys.setenv(fred_api_key = "your_api_key_here")

# Option 2: Add to .Renviron for permanent setup
usethis::edit_r_environ()
# Add line: fred_api_key=your_api_key_here

Quick Start

The package ships a six-year Treasury panel, so this runs as written:

library(dnsr)
data(treasury_yields)

# Fit the 750 most recent curves -- about three years, which is 36 month-ends,
# enough for the dynamics estimation below. "profile" solves the betas in
# closed form at each lambda, so it needs no start values.
dns_result <- fit_dns_model(treasury_yields, n_days = 750, method = "profile")
dns_result

# Factor dynamics, month-end sampled by default
dynamics <- estimate_dns_dynamics(dns_result$parameters)
dynamics

# Simulate forward from the most recent curve
latest <- dns_result$parameters[which.max(dns_result$parameters$Date), ]
params <- dns_dynamics_to_sim_params(dynamics, lambda = latest$lambda)

sim <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
  params = params,
  initial_factors = as.numeric(latest[c("beta1", "beta2", "beta3")]),
  maturities = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, 30),
  n_paths = 1000,
  engine = "exact"   # exact transition law; no YUIMA needed
)

# Discount factors and par yields off the fitted curve
factors <- matrix(as.numeric(latest[c("beta1", "beta2", "beta3")]), nrow = 1)
dns_discount_factors(factors, c(1, 5, 10, 30), latest$lambda)
dns_par_yields(factors, c(1, 5, 10, 30), latest$lambda)

Working with live data 

# Set FRED API key (do this once per session)
Sys.setenv(fred_api_key = "your_api_key_here")

library(dnsr)
yield_data <- get_treasury_yield_combined(start_date = "2020-01-01")

# Fit the DNS model
dns_result <- fit_dns_model(yield_data, n_days = 100)

# Visualize the results
plot_yield_curves(yield_data, dns_result)
factor_plots <- plot_factor_time_series(dns_result)
print(factor_plots$factors)

# Estimate factor dynamics
# (month-end sampling by default since 0.2.0; use sampling = "daily" for the
#  0.1.0 behavior)
dynamics <- estimate_dns_dynamics(dns_result$parameters)

# Simulate future yield curves with advanced SDE methods (requires YUIMA)
# get_treasury_yield_*() returns rows most-recent-first and fit_dns_model()
# keeps that order by default, so row 1 is the latest curve. Pass
# date_order = "ascending" if you would rather read it the other way round.
params <- dns_dynamics_to_sim_params(dynamics, lambda = dns_result$parameters$lambda[1])
initial_factors <- dns_result$parameters[1, c("beta1", "beta2", "beta3")]
maturities <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, 30)

sim_result <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
  params = params, 
  initial_factors = as.numeric(initial_factors),
  maturities = maturities,
  sim_method = "euler"  # Using YUIMA's Euler-Maruyama scheme
)

# Plot simulation results
yield_plots <- plot_simulated_yields(sim_result, time_points = c(0, 1, 5, 10))
print(yield_plots$yield_curves)

Advanced Stochastic Simulation

The package leverages the YUIMA framework for accurate simulation of stochastic differential equations. This provides:

  • Mathematical Rigor: Proper implementation of numerical SDE schemes (Euler-Maruyama, Milstein). The DNS diffusion does not depend on the state, so the two schemes coincide here; accuracy is set by n_steps.
  • Correlation Handling: Accurate simulation of correlated factors
  • Statistical Estimation: Advanced methods for parameter estimation

The factor system is a linear SDE, so its transition law over any step is a known Gaussian. engine = "exact" samples that law directly — no discretisation error at any step size, no YUIMA dependency, and about two orders of magnitude faster than one yuima::simulate() call per path:

params <- list(
  kappa = c(0.02, 0.3, 0.5),
  theta = c(0.04, -0.02, 0.01),
  sigma = c(0.005, 0.01, 0.02),
  correlation = diag(3)
)

sim_result <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
  params = params,
  initial_factors = c(0.045, -0.005, -0.015),
  maturities = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, 30),
  n_paths = 1000,
  engine = "exact"
)

The default is still engine = "yuima". The two agree in distribution, but they consume randomness differently, so a given seed does not reproduce the same paths across engines.

YUIMA also provides the quasi-maximum-likelihood estimator, as an alternative to the regression in estimate_dns_dynamics():

# A YUIMA model object, for analysis the package does not wrap
yuima_model <- dns_to_yuima_model(params)

# QMLE on the fitted factor series. A parameters frame can be passed straight
# in; its beta1/beta2/beta3 columns are picked out by name.
est_result <- estimate_dns_parameters_yuima(dns_result$parameters,
                                            delta_t = 1 / 252)
est_result$estimated_params

The Nelson-Siegel Model

The Nelson-Siegel model expresses the yield curve as:

y(m)=β1+β2(1−e−λmλm)+β3(1−e−λmλm−e−λm)y(m) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m}\right) + \beta_3 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m} - e^{-\lambda m}\right)

where: - y(m)y(m) is the yield at maturity mm - β1\beta_1 represents the long-term level of interest rates - β2\beta_2 represents the yield curve slope - β3\beta_3 represents the curvature - λ\lambda controls the decay rate of factor loadings

In the dynamic extension, the factors β1\beta_1, β2\beta_2, and β3\beta_3 are modeled as mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes:

dβi(t)=κi(θi−βi(t))dt+σidWi(t)d\beta_i(t) = \kappa_i(\theta_i - \beta_i(t))dt + \sigma_i dW_i(t)

Visualizations

Each plotting function returns ggplot objects (or a named list of them), so output can be themed, combined, or saved by the caller:

Function Shows
plot_yield_curves() Fitted curves against observed yields, with RMSE
plot_dns_loadings() Level, slope, and curvature loadings against maturity
plot_factor_time_series() Estimated factors over time, optionally as changes
plot_yield_surface() Yield surface across maturity and time
plot_yield_heatmap() Yield evolution as a maturity-by-time heatmap
plot_yield_pca() Principal components of the yield panel
plot_simulated_factors() Simulated factor paths
plot_simulated_yields() Simulated curves at selected horizons

Data

treasury_yields holds 1,501 daily U.S. Treasury curves across eleven maturities, 2 January 2019 to 31 December 2024, in decimal form. The source is FRED’s H.15 constant maturity series (DGS1MO through DGS30), which are U.S. government works in the public domain. data-raw/treasury_yields.R rebuilds it.

Applications

The dnsr package is useful for:

  • Interest Rate Risk Management: Model yield curve shifts for risk analysis
  • Economic Scenario Generation: Create consistent interest rate scenarios
  • Asset-Liability Management: Simulate future yield curves for ALM studies
  • Fixed Income Research: Analyze yield curve dynamics and factor behavior
  • Stress Testing: Generate extreme but plausible scenarios for risk management
